summary.text: A centered sawtooth bias is expanded by an Abel limit, turning its sum over squares into the limit as \(s\downarrow1\) of \(\sum_{a\ge1}\operatorname{Im}G_n(a)/a^s\); a gcd decomposition, CRT and spectral/determinant evaluations of odd Gauss sums together with explicit \(2\)-power evaluations reduce each part to a nonnegative constant times a real-character Dirichlet series, which is nonnegative by its Euler product. Thus the total bias is nonnegative, and bounding the number of nonzero square terms by \(n-1\) gives \(2\sum (k^2\bmod n)\le n(n-1)\), from which the claimed bound follows.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
e_n(y)=\exp(2\pi i y/n),\qquad
G_n(a)=\sum_{x\bmod n}e_n(ax^2).
\]
Here and below a sum over residues uses the representatives in \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\). We shall prove a positivity statement for quadratic Gauss sums, use it to obtain a nonnegative “quadratic residue bias,” and then turn that bias into the required inequality.

Throughout the proof, Dirichlet series may be written as sums over \(a\ge 0\), with the term at \(a=0\) understood to be zero. Equivalently, one may simply sum over \(a\ge1\).

## 1. Quadratic Gauss sums

We first establish the Gauss-sum information needed later.

### 1.1. Character orthogonality and elementary identities

The standard additive-character orthogonality relation is
\[
\sum_{x\bmod n}e_n(bx)=
\begin{cases}
n,&b\equiv0\pmod n,\\
0,&b\not\equiv0\pmod n.
\end{cases}                                      \tag{1}
\]
It follows either by summing a geometric progression or by translating the sum by a residue on which the character is nontrivial.

Two consequences that will be used repeatedly are as follows.

First, if \(d,n\ge1\), then
\[
G_{dn}(da)=dG_n(a).                                \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, write the residues modulo \(dn\) as \(x+ny\), with \(0\le x<n\) and \(0\le y<d\). The character \(e_{dn}(da(x+ny)^2)\) is independent of \(y\), and its value is \(e_n(ax^2)\).

Second, if \((m,n)=1\), the Chinese remainder parametrization
\[
(x,y)\longmapsto nx+my\pmod{mn}
\]
is bijective, because multiplication by \(n\) modulo \(m\), and by \(m\) modulo \(n\), are invertible. Expanding the square and observing that the mixed term is a multiple of \(mn\) gives
\[
G_{mn}(a)=G_m(an)G_n(am).                           \tag{3}
\]

### 1.2. Odd Gauss sums, including their phase

For odd \(N\), define \(\sigma_N(u)\in\{\pm1\}\), for a unit \(u\bmod N\), to be the sign of the permutation of \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\) given by multiplication by \(u\). Extend it to all residues by putting \(\sigma_N(u)=0\) for nonunits. This is a completely multiplicative character: composition of multiplication permutations corresponds to multiplication of units, and the sign of a composite is the product of the signs.

We claim that, for odd \(N\),
\[
G_N(1)=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt N,&N\equiv1\pmod4,\\
i\sqrt N,&N\equiv3\pmod4,
\end{cases}                                        \tag{4}
\]
and, for every unit \(u\bmod N\),
\[
G_N(u)=\sigma_N(u)G_N(1).                          \tag{5}
\]
We include the phase argument, since merely knowing \(|G_N(u)|=\sqrt N\) would not suffice for the later positivity proof.

Consider the normalized Fourier matrix, indexed by residues modulo \(N\),
\[
F_{r,s}=N^{-1/2}e_N(rs).
\]
By (1), \(F^*F=I\). A second application of (1) shows
\[
(F^2)_{r,s}=\begin{cases}1,&s=-r,\\0,&s\ne-r,\end{cases}
\]
and hence \(F^4=I\). If \(N\) is odd, the only fixed point of negation is \(0\), so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(F^2)=1.                          \tag{6}
\]
Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(F)=N^{-1/2}G_N(1).               \tag{7}
\]

The usual change of variables \((x,y)\mapsto(x-y,x+y)\), which is bijective because \(2\) is invertible modulo odd \(N\), gives
\[
G_N(1)\overline{G_N(1)}
 =\sum_{x,y}e_N(x^2-y^2)
 =\sum_{r,s}e_N(rs)=N                             \tag{8}
\]
by (1). Thus \(|\operatorname{tr}(F)|=1\).

It remains to determine the determinant of \(F\). Write \(N=2m+1\). The unnormalized Fourier matrix is the Vandermonde matrix formed from
\(1,e_N(1),\ldots,e_N(N-1)\), so its determinant is
\[
\prod_{0\le r<s<N}(e_N(s)-e_N(r)).                 \tag{9}
\]
For \(r<s\), the elementary sine factorization gives
\[
e_N(s)-e_N(r)
 =i\exp\!\left(\frac{\pi i(r+s)}N\right)
   2\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi(s-r)}N\right).          \tag{10}
\]
Every sine factor here is positive. There are
\( inom N2=Nm\) pairs. Furthermore,
\[
\sum_{0\le r<s<N}(r+s)=2Nm^2.
\]
Consequently the product of all exponential factors in (10) is
\(\exp(2\pi i m^2)=1\). Thus the determinant of the unnormalized matrix is \(i^{Nm}\) times a positive real number. Normalization only multiplies it by a positive real number. Since \(F\) is unitary, its determinant has modulus one, and therefore
\[
\det F=i^{Nm}.                                      \tag{11}
\]

We now extract the trace from (6), (8), and (11). Since \(F\) is unitary and \(F^4=I\), its eigenvalues belong to \(\{1,-1,i,-i\}\). Let their multiplicities be \(A,B,C,D\), respectively. Then
\[
A+B+C+D=2m+1,                                      \tag{12}
\]
\[
A+B-C-D=\operatorname{tr}(F^2)=1,                 \tag{13}
\]
\[
\operatorname{tr}(F)=(A-B)+(C-D)i,                \tag{14}
\]
and
\[
\det F=i^{2B+C+3D}=i^{(2m+1)m}.                   \tag{15}
\]
Because the trace has modulus one, (14) yields
\[
(A-B)^2+(C-D)^2=1.                                 \tag{16}
\]
The two integer differences in (16) are therefore one of
\((\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)\). Equations (12) and (13), together with the determinant congruence (15) modulo \(4\), leave exactly two possibilities:
\[
A=B+1,\quad C=D,\quad m\text{ even},              \tag{17}
\]
or
\[
A=B,\quad C=D+1,\quad m\text{ odd}.               \tag{18}
\]
This is a direct four-case calculation: (13) says
\((A-B)+(C-D)=1\), so among the four possibilities from (16) only
\((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) remain; substituting each into (15) determines the parity of \(m\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{tr}(F)=
\begin{cases}1,&m\text{ even},\\i,&m\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(m\) is even exactly when \(N\equiv1\pmod4\), (7) proves (4).

For a unit \(u\), let
\[
F_u(r,s)=N^{-1/2}e_N(urs).
\]
This is obtained from \(F\) by permuting rows by multiplication by \(u\). The same orthogonality calculation gives
\[
F_u^*F_u=I,\qquad F_u^2(r,s)=1_{s=-r},\qquad F_u^4=I,
\]
so \(\operatorname{tr}(F_u^2)=1\). Also
\[
\operatorname{tr}(F_u)=N^{-1/2}G_N(u),
\quad |\operatorname{tr}(F_u)|=1,
\]
and row permutation gives
\[
\det F_u=\sigma_N(u)i^{Nm}.                        \tag{19}
\]
If \(\sigma_N(u)=1\), the preceding eigenvalue-multiplicity argument applies unchanged and gives \(\operatorname{tr}(F_u)=\operatorname{tr}(F)\). If \(\sigma_N(u)=-1\), apply the same argument to \(-F_u\): because the dimension \(N\) is odd, its determinant is
\(-\det F_u=i^{Nm}\), while its square, fourth power, and trace norm have the same required values. Thus \(\operatorname{tr}(-F_u)=\operatorname{tr}(F)\), or \(\operatorname{tr}(F_u)=-\operatorname{tr}(F)\). This proves (5).

We will also need the value of this sign character at \(2\):
\[
\sigma_N(2)=\chi_8(N),                             \tag{20}
\]
where, for odd \(N\), \(\chi_8(N)=1\) if \(N\equiv1,7\pmod8\), and \(-1\) if \(N\equiv3,5\pmod8\).

For completeness, write \(N=2m+1\) and represent residues by \(0,1,\ldots,2m\). Multiplication by \(2\) sends \(r\) to
\[
2r\quad(r\le m),\qquad 2r-N\quad(r>m).
\]
For a fixed \(s>m\), the earlier index \(r<s\) forms an inversion with \(s\) exactly when
\[
s-m\le r\le m.
\]
Thus the total number \(E\) of inversions satisfies
\[
2E=m(m+1).
\]
Checking \(m\) modulo \(4\) gives
\((-1)^E=1,-1,-1,1\) for \(N\equiv1,3,5,7\pmod8\), respectively, which is exactly (20).

### 1.3. The power-of-two factor

Let \(\chi_4(a)\) denote the real character modulo \(4\), equal to \(1\) for \(a\equiv1\pmod4\), \(-1\) for \(a\equiv3\pmod4\), and \(0\) for even \(a\). Let \(\chi_8\) be the analogous real character modulo \(8\), equal to \(1\) on \(1,7\), \(-1\) on \(3,5\), and \(0\) on even residues.

For odd \(a\), direct summation modulo \(2,4,8\) gives
\[
G_2(a)=0,                                           \tag{21}
\]
\[
G_4(a)=2\bigl(1+i\chi_4(a)\bigr),                 \tag{22}
\]
and
\[
G_8(a)=2\sqrt2\,\chi_8(a)
       \bigl(1+i\chi_4(a)\bigr).                  \tag{23}
\]
Indeed, the squares modulo \(4\) are \(0,1,0,1\), while modulo \(8\) the even squares are \(0\) or \(4\) and every odd square is \(1\); inserting the eighth roots of unity yields these formulas.

For every \(M\ge1\) and odd \(a\), grouping residues modulo \(16M\) according to their class modulo \(4M\) gives
\[
G_{16M}(a)=2G_{4M}(a).                              \tag{24}
\]
Here is the cancellation explicitly. Write a residue as \(x+4My\), \(0\le y<4\). Expanding the square shows that the corresponding character equals the \(x\)-term times \(e_2(axy)\). Summing over \(y\) is \(4\) if \(x\) is even and \(0\) if \(x\) is odd. Put \(x=2z\); then the remaining character is the one modulo \(4M\) at \(z\). On the other hand, splitting the sum modulo \(4M\) into the two lifts of residues modulo \(2M\) shows that \(G_{4M}(a)\) is twice its corresponding half-range sum. Comparing the two expressions gives (24).

Induction from (22), (23), and (24) now yields, for \(k\ge0\) and odd \(a\),
\[
G_{2^{k+2}}(a)
 =\sqrt{2^{k+2}}\,\chi_8(a)^{k+2}
    \bigl(1+i\chi_4(a)\bigr).                     \tag{25}
\]
The induction proceeds in steps of two: increasing the exponent by two doubles both the Gauss sum and the square-root factor, while \(\chi_8(a)^2=1\) for odd \(a\).

### 1.4. The imaginary part for a general modulus

Write every \(n\ge1\) uniquely as
\[
n=2^j t,
\]
where \(t\) is odd. We claim that there are a completely multiplicative function
\(\chi:\mathbb N\to\{0,1,-1\}\) and a constant \(c\ge0\), depending on \(n\), such that
\[
1_{(a,n)=1}\,\Im G_n(a)=c\chi(a)                  \tag{26}
\]
for every \(a\ge1\).

There are three cases.

If \(j=0\), formula (4)-(5) says that for \((a,t)=1\),
\[
G_t(a)=\sigma_t(a)
\begin{cases}\sqrt t,&t\equiv1\pmod4,\\i\sqrt t,&t\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus if \(t\equiv1\pmod4\), take \(c=0\) and \(\chi=1\). If \(t\equiv3\pmod4\), take \(c=\sqrt t\) and \(\chi=\sigma_t\), extended by zero at nonunits.

If \(j=1\), then for \((a,2t)=1\), (3) contains the factor \(G_2(at)=0\) from (21). Hence again take \(c=0\).

Finally suppose \(j=k+2\ge2\). For \((a,n)=1\), the numbers \(a\) and \(t\) are odd. Combining the CRT identity (3), the odd formula (4)-(5), the power-of-two formula (25), and \(\sigma_t(2)=\chi_8(t)\), one obtains
\[
\Im G_n(a)=\sqrt n\,\sigma_t(a)\chi_8(a)^{k+2}
\begin{cases}
\chi_4(a),&t\equiv1\pmod4,\\
1,&t\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases}                                        \tag{27}
\]
The factors involving \(t\) that arise from CRT cancel because their squares are one; taking the imaginary part of
\((1+i\chi_4(a))\) or \(i(1-i\chi_4(a))\) gives precisely the displayed two cases. Therefore (26) holds with \(c=\sqrt n\) and
\[
\chi(a)=\sigma_t(a)\chi_8(a)^{k+2}
\begin{cases}
\chi_4(a),&t\equiv1\pmod4,\\
1,&t\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
Each factor is completely multiplicative and has absolute value at most one. If \((a,n)>1\), either \((a,t)>1\), making \(\sigma_t(a)=0\), or \(a\) is even, making the positive power of \(\chi_8(a)\) zero. Thus (26) also has the correct zero value off the units.

## 2. Positivity of the Gauss-sum Dirichlet series

We next prove that for every \(n\ge1\) and every real \(s>1\),
\[
\sum_{a\ge1}\Im G_n(a)\,a^{-s}\ge0.               \tag{28}
\]

First consider only coefficients coprime to \(n\). By (26), their series is
\[
c\sum_{a\ge1}\chi(a)a^{-s}.                       \tag{29}
\]
The latter series converges absolutely because \(|\chi(a)|\le1\). Since \(\chi\) is completely multiplicative, its Euler product is
\[
\sum_{a\ge1}\chi(a)a^{-s}
 =\prod_p\frac1{1-\chi(p)p^{-s}}.                  \tag{30}
\]
Each factor is nonnegative—in fact positive—because \(\chi(p)\in[-1,1]\) and \(p^{-s}<1\). Finite partial products are therefore nonnegative, and their limit is nonnegative. Since \(c\ge0\), the series restricted to \((a,n)=1\) is nonnegative.

To pass from units to all coefficients, partition the positive integers according to
\(d=(a,n)\), where \(d\mid n\), and write \(a=db\). Then
\[
(db,n)=d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (b,n/d)=1.   \tag{31}
\]
Using (2),
\[
G_n(db)=dG_{n/d}(b).                                \tag{32}
\]
Therefore the contribution from the stratum \((a,n)=d\) is
\[
\sum_{(a,n)=d}\Im G_n(a)a^{-s}
=d^{1-s}\sum_{(b,n/d)=1}\Im G_{n/d}(b)b^{-s}.      \tag{33}
\]
The factor \(d^{1-s}\) is nonnegative, and the inner sum is nonnegative by the unit case. Summing (33) over all divisors \(d\mid n\) proves (28). Absolute convergence, needed for these rearrangements, follows from the elementary bound
\[
|G_n(a)|\le n,                                     \tag{34}
\]
since \(G_n(a)\) is a sum of \(n\) complex numbers of modulus one.

## 3. A boundary value of the geometric Dirichlet series

Define, for a residue \(y\bmod n\),
\[
B_n(y)=
\begin{cases}
0,&y=0,\\[2mm]
\displaystyle\frac12-\frac{r}{n},&y\ne0,
\end{cases}                                        \tag{35}
\]
where \(r\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is the least nonnegative representative of \(y\). We shall connect this bias with additive characters.

The needed analytic identity is
\[
\lim_{s\downarrow1}\sum_{a\ge1}\Im(z^a)a^{-s}
 =\Im\bigl(-\log(1-z)\bigr)                        \tag{36}
\]
for \(|z|=1\), \(z\ne1\), using the principal logarithm.

Here is a proof that also justifies passage to the boundary. The partial sums of \(z,z^2,\ldots\) satisfy
\[
\left|\sum_{a=1}^m z^a\right|
 =\left|z\frac{z^m-1}{z-1}\right|
 \le \frac2{|z-1|}.                                \tag{37}
\]
For \(1\le s\le2\), summation by parts expresses
\(\sum_{a\ge1}z^aa^{-s}\) as
\[
\sum_{r\ge0}\bigl((r+1)^{-s}-(r+2)^{-s}\bigr)
       \sum_{a=1}^{r+1}z^a.                        \tag{38}
\]
The mean value theorem gives the uniform bound
\[
\left|(r+1)^{-s}-(r+2)^{-s}\right|
 \le2(r+1)^{-2}.                                   \tag{39}
\]
Together with (37), this makes (38) uniformly convergent for \(1\le s\le2\), so it is continuous at \(s=1\). For \(s>1\), (38) is just the absolutely convergent series \(\sum z^aa^{-s}\). At \(s=1\), the power-series identity
\[
\sum_{a\ge1}\frac{w^a}{a}=-\log(1-w),\qquad |w|<1,
\]
followed by radial passage \(w=rz\to z\), gives the value \(-\log(1-z)\). The point \(1-z\) does not cross the branch cut: since \(|z|=1\) and \(z\ne1\), one has \(\Re z<1\), hence \(\Re(1-z)>0\). This proves (36).

Now take
\[
z=e_n(y).
\]
If \(y=0\), every imaginary part is zero and the desired limit is zero. If \(y\ne0\), write \(y=r\) with \(1\le r<n\), and put \(\theta=\pi r/n\), so \(0<\theta<\pi\) and \(z=e^{2i\theta}\). The elementary factorization
\[
1-e^{2i\theta}=2\sin\theta\,e^{i(\theta-\pi/2)}
\]
has a positive real factor \(2\sin\theta\), and \(\theta-\pi/2\in(-\pi,\pi)\). Hence the principal argument of \(1-e^{2i\theta}\) is \(\theta-\pi/2\), and therefore
\[
\Im\bigl(-\log(1-e^{2i\theta})\bigr)
 =\frac\pi2-\theta
 =\pi\left(\frac12-\frac rn\right).
\]
Combining this with (36) gives, for every residue \(y\),
\[
\lim_{s\downarrow1}
 \sum_{a\ge1}\Im e_n(ay)\,a^{-s}
 =\pi B_n(y).                                      \tag{40}
\]

Choose, for example, the sequence
\[
s_m=1+\frac1{m+1},
\]
so \(1<s_m\le2\) and \(s_m\to1\). Sum (40) over all residues \(x\bmod n\), with \(y=x^2\). This is a finite sum, so limits may be interchanged with the sum over \(x\). For each fixed \(s_m>1\), absolute convergence permits interchanging the finite residue sum and the series over \(a\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x\bmod n}\sum_{a\ge1}
  \Im e_n(ax^2)a^{-s_m}
&=\sum_{a\ge1}\Im\left(\sum_{x\bmod n}e_n(ax^2)\right)a^{-s_m}\\
&=\sum_{a\ge1}\Im G_n(a)a^{-s_m}.
\end{aligned}                                      \tag{41}
\]
By (28), the right-hand side is nonnegative. Passing to the limit in (41), and using (40), yields
\[
0\le \pi\sum_{x\bmod n}B_n(x^2).
\]
Since \(\pi>0\),
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \sum_{x\bmod n}B_n(x^2)\ge0.} \tag{42}
\]

## 4. From bias to the residue-sum bound

For every residue \(y\), definition (35) can be rewritten as
\[
B_n(y)=1_{y\ne0}\frac12-\frac{\operatorname{val}(y)}n, \tag{43}
\]
because \(\operatorname{val}(0)=0\). Applying (43) to \(y=x^2\), summing, and using (42), gives
\[
\frac1n\sum_{x\bmod n}\operatorname{val}(x^2)
\le \frac12\#\{x\bmod n:x^2\ne0\}.               \tag{44}
\]
The residue \(x=0\) certainly has square zero, so there are at most \(n-1\) residues with nonzero square. (There may be additional square-zero residues when \(n\) is not squarefree; this only strengthens the estimate.) Hence
\[
\frac1n\sum_{x\bmod n}\operatorname{val}(x^2)
\le\frac{n-1}{2}.
\]
Multiplying by \(2n>0\),
\[
2\sum_{x\bmod n}\operatorname{val}(x^2)
\le n(n-1).                                        \tag{45}
\]

The representatives \(x=0,1,\ldots,n-1\) enumerate all residues modulo \(n\), and
\[
\operatorname{val}(x^2)=x^2\bmod n.
\]
Therefore, if
\[
A(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k^2\bmod n),
\]
then (45) says
\[
2A(n)\le n(n-1).                                   \tag{46}
\]
This is the same sequence as the sum from \(k=1\) through \(n\), because the omitted term \(0^2\bmod n\) and the added term \(n^2\bmod n\) are both zero.

Finally, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
n(n-1)=n^2-n\le n^2-1.
\]
Thus
\[
2A(n)\le n^2-1.                                    \tag{47}
\]
Since \(A(n)\) is an integer, (47) is equivalent to
\[
A(n)\le \left\lfloor\frac{n^2-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
The quotient in the statement is integer division, i.e. precisely this floor. Consequently, for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle A(n)\le\frac{n^2-1}{2}}
\]
in the intended integer-division sense.
